name: Pedro Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying to be a primary school teacher, so my week is education lectures, a day a week in a real classroom and a lot of reading about how children learn. I'm in a student flat with two lads from my home town, Cáceres, and we all go to Mass on Sunday if we're not too tired. My dad owns a hardware shop and my mum sings in the church choir, and they pay for everything. I've never used any of these chatbots, and I like writing my lesson plans on paper first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that's what I thought, a lot of noise for nothing. I'd say it at my parents' dinner table and my dad would nod. I'd say there's no substitute for a good teacher in front of children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel vindicated, to be honest. I've been uncomfortable with everyone telling me I must use these tools, because I think children learn from people. I'd be happy if schools stopped chasing gadgets and went back to basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd work on my handwriting for the board, my voice, and how I keep a class's attention. I'd try to spend more time with my placement teacher, Señora Ruiz, because she's the best I've seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like the pace of it, and I can see where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Señora Ruiz do that you think no machine could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was a boy in my placement teacher's class who hadn't spoken for a week, and she noticed because he stopped drawing. She knelt down and asked him about his dog, and by the end of the day he was talking. A screen couldn't have seen that he'd stopped drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said schools should go back to basics. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading aloud, handwriting, times tables, learning poems by heart, and respect for the teacher. I think too many schools have bought tablets and forgotten the children need to sit still and listen. I don't hate technology, but I don't think it should lead the lesson.

say: I'd say it was **a lot of noise** and nothing replaces a teacher in front of children.
I'd say it at my parents' **dinner table**, where my dad would nod.
think: I feel **vindicated**, because children learn from people, not gadgets.
I'd be happy if schools went **back to basics**.
do: Carry on as I am and work on my **voice and handwriting** for the board.
Spend more time with my placement teacher, **Señora Ruiz**.
feel: I feel **calm**, because I like the pace and can see where I'm going.
S0.quote: There was a boy in my placement teacher's class who hadn't spoken for a week, and she noticed because he stopped drawing
fieldNote: His **resistance** to technology comes from a belief that teaching is about people, with a real classroom example.
His traditional outlook shows in **back to basics**: handwriting, reading aloud and respect.
No money pressure and a clear vocation make him **calm** in a quiet world.

steps.text: Spend extra placement time with Señora Ruiz

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change for offices and shops, but teaching will be fine because children need adults. I'd say people should keep real skills, like how to fix things and how to talk to others. I'd say it carefully, because I don't actually know much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried about what it does to children, more than to my job. If kids get used to a machine answering everything, will they learn to think? And I worry my dad's shop will lose customers to online stores that use more of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and maybe ask my tutors how schools are meant to use it, so I'm not caught out. I wouldn't use it myself unless I had to. I'd talk with my dad about whether to add an online shop, and offer to help him in the holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's mostly for the children and the shop, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your dad add an online shop. How do you square that with avoiding technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit of a contradiction, I know. But the shop is family, and I'd rather help it survive than be proud. I'd learn just enough to set up a basic order page, and ask my cousin Jorge, who's good with computers, to do the hard bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the parents of your future pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, read to your children every night and let them be bored sometimes. I'd say a child needs to struggle with a hard sentence before a machine finishes it for them. I'd ask them to trust me with the hours at school and take care of the habits at home.

say: I'd say teaching will be fine because **children need adults**.
I'd tell people to keep **real skills** like fixing things and talking.
think: I'm worried what it does to **children's thinking** more than to my job.
I fear my dad's shop will lose customers to **online stores**.
do: Ask my tutors how schools are meant to use it, so I'm **not caught out**.
Help my dad set up a **basic online shop** with my cousin Jorge.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, mostly for the children and the shop.
S1.quote: A child needs to struggle with a hard sentence before a machine finishes it for them
fieldNote: His worry is about **children and family**, not about his own post.
He admits the **contradiction** of helping an online shop while avoiding technology himself.
Cousin Jorge is his **bridge** to technology, which fits a resistant person who relies on family.

steps.text: Help Dad set up a basic online order page
Ask tutors how primary schools should use AI
Ask my cousin Jorge to do the technical parts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we should all slow down and pray about it. I'd say it at church and at home. I'd say governments have to protect families and small businesses before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. If thinking work is gone by 2028, then children's futures look uncertain and what we teach them seems less sure. And my dad's shop, which is hands-on, might survive until 2031, but the ordering and paperwork would be done by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my course, because a teacher is a person, and I'd lean on my family and church community. I'd help my dad in the shop at weekends and learn how his stock system works. And I'd vote for whoever speaks up for families, even if I normally don't care for politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot, and I'd want to be close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents to do in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the shop as debt-free as possible and not take any risks. My dad wants to expand next year, but I'd ask him to wait. I'd also ask him to hold on to savings in cash or gold, not in anything that might disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your faith change how you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does help. My priest says work was meant to give us dignity, not just money, and I hold on to that. If machines do the work, then the question is how we take care of each other, and that is something the church knows how to do.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and we should slow down and pray about it.
I'd say governments must **protect families** and small businesses.
think: I'm anxious that **children's futures** look uncertain and teaching feels less sure.
My dad's shop might survive hands-on, but **ordering and paperwork** go to machines.
do: Stay in my course and **lean on** my family and church.
Help my dad in the shop and learn his **stock system**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, praying a lot and wanting to be close to home.
S2.quote: My dad wants to expand next year, but I'd ask him to wait
fieldNote: His response is to **retreat** to family, church and caution, consistent with a resistant, traditional person.
Faith offers a **frame** for work and dignity, and a community that can respond.
His anxiety is about **children** and the family shop, not his own job.

steps.text: Ask Dad to postpone the shop expansion and avoid debt
Learn the shop's stock system on weekends
Lean on the parish and family for support
Vote for the party that backs families and small shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and we should prepare, but not panic. I'd say families should keep their savings and stay close to each other. I'd say schools need to keep teaching the basics, because children will need character most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I'd qualify and start teaching just as thinking AI arrives. I'd have a job in a school, probably, because parents want a human with their kids. I think my job might be one of the safest, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a job in a local school and maybe help at church with the youth group. I'd save part of my salary and keep helping my dad. I'd also learn a little about whatever the school uses, since I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'm okay, but I don't like the feeling of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn a little about what the school uses. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit like taking medicine. I'd do it because it's part of the job, not because I like it. I'd ask the older teachers, and I'd try to learn it at the pace that suits me, not the one the headteacher wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young person who wants to do an apprenticeship instead of university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go for it, especially if it's a trade with hands. Plumbers, electricians and carpenters will be needed longer than office workers. I'd say my own cousin is a carpenter's apprentice and he'll earn as much as me in five years, without debt.

say: I'd say it's serious, but families should **keep their savings** and stay close.
I'd say schools should keep teaching **the basics** and character.
think: I'd qualify just as **thinking AI** arrives, and my job might be among the safest.
Parents will still want a **human** with their children.
do: Finish the degree and take a **local school job**.
Save part of my **salary** and keep helping my dad.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, and I don't like the feeling of waiting.
S3.quote: Plumbers, electricians and carpenters will be needed longer than office workers
fieldNote: His **traditional** view favours apprenticeships and trades, which he backs with a cousin's example.
He treats AI learning like **medicine**: accepted because it is part of the job.
He thinks teaching is safe but is **not certain**, so his mood stays uneasy.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply to local primary schools
Save part of my first salary each month
Learn the school's tools from older teachers at my own pace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, we have time to keep what matters. I'd say it's a chance to teach children well, and to get ready without losing our way of life. I'd say families should stay strong, and the rest will sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit uneasy, because change is change. But ten years lets me become a good teacher, marry, maybe have children and buy a flat before the hands-on robots in 2039. I'd feel like I'd done what I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, teach, and probably marry my girlfriend Lucía. I'd save for a flat and keep helping my dad's shop. I'd also volunteer at church with children, so the community stays tight. And I'd learn the tools slowly, only when the school requires them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small knot. I like having time, but I still don't trust the direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the small knot about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's whether the world my children grow up in will have the same values. I don't mind new gadgets, but I mind a world where nobody has time for each other. I'd like to have kids who still know their grandparents' village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is ten years different from five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'm starting from nothing, with ten years I'm settled. I could be married, have a bit saved and a place in the community. That's where I'd rather be when the big change comes.

say: I'd say **we have time** to keep what matters and teach children well.
I'd say **families** should stay strong and the rest sorts itself out.
think: I'm still a bit uneasy, but ten years lets me be a **good teacher** and settle down.
I'd marry, save for a **flat**, and be settled before 2039.
do: Qualify, teach and **marry Lucía**, then save for a flat.
Volunteer with children at **church** and learn the tools only when the school requires.
feel: I feel **calm**, with a small knot about the direction.
S4.quote: With five years I'm starting from nothing, with ten years I'm settled
fieldNote: Ten years turns the threat into a **life plan** with marriage, a flat and a community role.
His small knot is about **values**, not jobs, which is typical of his traditional outlook.
He relies on **community** more than on any tool or policy.

steps.text: Qualify and teach at a local primary school
Save for a flat deposit with Lucía
Volunteer with the parish children's group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because families and small shops can't change in two years. What would help is a government that backs families, keeps small businesses alive and protects what children learn, plus a community that looks after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I just think we should ask what it's for, and whether it helps families stay together. If it doesn't, it isn't worth much to me.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I just think we should ask what it's for, and whether it helps families stay together
portrait: Pedro is a 19-year-old **primary teaching** student from Cáceres whose family pays for everything.
He has never used **AI tools** and writes lesson plans on paper, believing children learn from people.
Traditional in outlook, he backs **apprenticeships**, faith and family and wants to protect small shops.
His mood moves from calm to **anxious** at 2028, mostly for his father's hardware shop and children's futures.
With ten years he sees a settled life: marriage, a flat and a role in his community.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because families and small shops can't change in two years.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a government that **backs families**, keeps small businesses alive and protects what children learn.
